Vanna: Vanna is composable, undercollateralized credit infrastructure for DeFi
Vanna: Maximum leverage is 10×
Vanna: Liquidation threshold / health-factor floor is 1.1×
Vanna: Health factor = total collateral USD / total debt USD, never stored, derived on demand, WAD precision
Vanna: Protocol comprises 14 Soroban smart contracts in five groups
Vanna: Every user gets their own deployed SmartAccount contract with its own storage; a bug in one cannot affect another
Vanna: Lending pools are separate contracts per asset; a problem in one cannot affect another
Vanna: Rate model is a smooth polynomial with no kink point: APR = 3.5 × (u·0.1 + u³²·0.1 + u⁶⁴·0.3)
Vanna: Approximate borrow APRs: ~9% at 25% util · ~18% at 50% · ~28% at 80% · ~33% at 90% · ~44% at 95% · ~115% at 99%
Vanna: Pool equilibrium typically settles at 70–85% utilization
Vanna: No governance votes and no fixed rates — the rate responds to pool state in real time
Vanna: Oracle is a passthrough to Reflector, ~5-minute update cadence
Vanna: Registry-based address resolution; no hardcoded addresses in business logic
Vanna: All rounding uses floor division (mul_wad_down/div_wad_down) to prevent rounding in the protocol's favour
Vanna: Debt in health checks uses raw borrow shares, slightly understating true debt between pool operations; the 1.1× threshold is the buffer
Vanna: Liquidation clears all debt in one transaction — partial liquidation is not supported
Vanna: There is currently no liquidation fee
Vanna: liquidate() requires the account owner's authorization
Vanna: sweep_to() transfers XLM and USDC balances; Blend b-tokens and Aquarius LP positions are not unwound — records cleared, assets remain in the external protocol
Vanna: Bad debt reduces the pool's total_assets, dropping the vToken exchange rate and distributing the shortfall proportionally across LPs
Vanna: Integrated external protocols on testnet: Blend Capital, Aquarius, Soroswap
Vanna: Assets on testnet: XLM and USDC (plus Aquarius USDC and Soroswap USDC variants)
Vanna: All contracts are on Stellar Testnet. Mainnet addresses will be published at launch.
Vanna: Four documented delta-neutral strategies with risk/complexity ratings
Vanna: Docs explicitly state strategies minimise price and liquidation risk, not protocol risk
Vanna: Events indexed via Mercury
Vanna: TypeScript SDK is @vanna/sdk; docs use the Stellar SDK and Freighter wallet
Vanna: Site displays: 15+ integrations · 6+ chains · 1,000+ users

Vanna: Ecosystem logos: Stellar, Hyperliquid, Uniswap, Optimism (via Derive), Soroswap, ZeroDev, Katana, Avantis, Draper University, Morpho, Privy, Blend, Aerodrome, Derive, Gitcoin, Aquarius, Aster, Pivot Ventures
Vanna: Site footer: "Built on Stellar · Base · Arbitrum · Optimism"
Vanna: Site legal line: positions at outside venues remain subject to those venues' own margin and liquidation rules
Vanna: Published tool taxonomy — READ: get_account_state, estimate_capacity, simulate_position · WRITE: open_position, repay_debt, rebalance · RISK: protect_position, get_risk_alerts
Vanna: "Scoped session keys · Vanna never holds custody · the guardian runs beneath all three"
Vanna: GitHub org has 4 public repos, all website-related; protocol contracts are not public
Vanna: docs.vanna.finance/security/ reads "Coming Soon"
Vanna: x402 and MPP are both live on Stellar mainnet; SDF is a Premier member of the x402 Foundation
Vanna: ~100M x402 payments on Base; $1+ transactions rose from 49% to 95% of volume in a year
Vanna: Galaxy Research estimates agentic commerce at $3–5T B2C revenue by 2030
Vanna: MPP launched with 100+ integrated services incl. Stripe, Anthropic, OpenAI, Shopify, Visa; spec submitted to IETF
Vanna: The self-collateralization principle: borrowed capital cannot leave the margin account, so the borrow guard counts it on both sides. (Tier B — design/architecture, on testnet)
Vanna: TrackingToken lets the RiskEngine value external Blend/Aquarius/Soroswap positions as collateral. (Tier B — design/architecture, on testnet)

Vanna: Blend b-tokens are converted to underlying via b_rate then priced by the oracle; after conversion a Blend USDC position and a direct USDC deposit are treated identically. (Tier B — design/architecture, on testnet)
Vanna: SmartAccount rejects all calls not originating from its registered AccountManager. (Tier B — design/architecture, on testnet)
Vanna: Closed accounts are recycled into an inactive pool and reused to save deployment cost. (Tier B — design/architecture, on testnet)
Vanna: Lite Mode executes deposit + borrow + deploy-to-yield in a single transaction. (Tier B — design/architecture, on testnet)
Vanna: MCP server is zero-custody with a separate Sign Service as the only signer, using scoped session keys and spend caps. (Tier B — design/architecture, on testnet)

This arc argues the missing primitive is credit, not payments. ## What it may claim The lead framing is the one that survived the August 2026 repositioning: **"Morpho gives agents access to a lending market. # Capital efficiency **"Your collateral is doing one job. It should be doing six."** Isolated pools fragment collateral. The same capital, posted once into a unified margin account, can support several positions at once. This arc argues the waste is the story: not that borrowing is unavailable, but that it is needlessly expensive in capital terms. ## What it may claim The unified margin mechanism and the borrowing capacity it unlocks, stated at the tier the ledger allows. Multiples such as "up to 10x" are illustrative and must be labelled as such — see [/facts/tier-b-qualified.md](/facts/tier-b-qualified.md). ## Where it must not go - No TVL, no user counts, no realised returns (`P1-tvl`, `P4-demo-as-result`). - A capacity figure without an illustrative label trips `C-unlabelled-demo`. - "10x" alongside credit or borrow language without testnet disclosure raises `A-missing-testnet`. ## How it argues against the others Against [risk relief](/arcs/risk-relief.md): a floor that never gets tested is insurance nobody needed. Most users are not being liquidated — they are over-collateralised and under-deployed, and that cost is paid every single day rather than on a bad one. Against [age

# Narrative arcs Three competing positions, one per strategist. Assigned rather than chosen, so the agents must argue instead of converge. * [Capital efficiency](/arcs/capital-efficiency.md) - collateral doing one job * [Risk relief](/arcs/risk-relief.md) - surviving leverage, not acquiring it * [Agentic credit](/arcs/agentic-credit.md) - agents can pay, cannot borrow

# Risk relief **"Leverage is easy. Not getting liquidated is the hard part."** The reader already has access to leverage from a dozen places. What they do not have is a mechanism that keeps them solvent while they sleep. This arc argues that the scarce thing is survival, not access. ## What it may claim Only what the facts ledger supports. The concrete, quotable mechanisms are the 1.1x health-factor floor rather than 1.0x, the oracle cadence, and per-account contract isolation. See [/facts/tier-a-quotable.md](/facts/tier-a-quotable.md). ## Where it must not go - It may not promise that liquidation is prevented. It is reduced within a policy the user sets. `P5-returns-promise` in [/rules/hard-prohibitions.md](/rules/hard-prohibitions.md) blocks the stronger framing. - It may not present a demo figure as a realised outcome (`P4-demo-as-result`). - Any post touching leverage or credit must disclose testnet status, per [/company/constraint.md](/company/constraint.md). ## How it argues against the others Against [capital efficiency](/arcs/capital-efficiency.md): more efficient collateral is more collateral at risk in one place. Efficiency without a floor is a faster route to liquidation

# Brand palette The values the card renderer uses. Changing them here documents the intent; `render_visual.py` lines 48–57 and 155 are still where they take effect, so change both until the renderer reads this concept. ## Replacing these for another company Replace the whole set together. The accents were chosen against a very dark background (`#0D0616`) and will not survive a light one unaltered — a light theme needs new accent values, not the same ones on a new backdrop. Drop the new logo at the path in `logo`. **If it is missing the render still succeeds with an empty brand block**, so check the produced card rather than trusting the exit code. Card geometry is fixed at 1080×1080 in two places: the CSS body rule and Chrome's `--window-size`. Changing one without the other produces a cropped or letterboxed card. ## Provenance The dark social theme was derived from the product cards `cl-11` and `cl-16` in `design references/`. Note that `design references/theme.md` documents the company's **light** application system — it is not a spec for these cards. The renderer is currently the only specification of the dark social variant, which is why this concept exists.
# Channels Where content goes, and who has to approve it first. * [Telegram human review](/channels/telegram-review.md) - blocking approval gate * [X (Twitter)](/channels/x.md) - publishing target

# Telegram human review The last gate before anything reaches a platform, and the product's safety story. Any reply that is neither an approval nor a rejection is kept as revision notes and the draft becomes `changes_requested`. In OKF terms this is what produces a **human-reviewed** trust tier: an approval here is the `verified: { by: human:<id> }` event on the resulting post. **Known defect:** the orchestrator overrides the 3600s default down to 120s, and 7 of 13 recorded runs ended `timeout` as a result. The two-minute window encodes an assumption nobody stated.

# X (Twitter) Published through OpenCLI's Chrome bridge, which drives a logged-in browser profile rather than an API. **The account is a personal handle, not a brand handle.** For a company other than the operator's own, per-tenant account ownership is an open question with legal as well as technical parts — settle it before the first publish. **Failure modes:** a 60s `TIMEOUT`, and `No SW` when the daemon is alive but no extension service worker is attached, which breaks reads as well as writes. A timeout is not proof the post failed — read the timeline before retrying or you will double-post.

# Positioning directive — infrastructure-led, dual B2B + B2C **A standing directive. Every arc, every post, every launch plan honours it.** ## The directive User acquisition continues, but it is no longer the headline. The **major emphasis is the infrastructure Vanna is building**: composable credit rails that are **scalable, flexible, reliable, and versatile**, and that serve **both B2B and B2C** from one system — businesses embedding credit into their own product, and end users (and their agents) getting a credit account — **without changing the underlying system**. Position Vanna as the *solution both ecosystems build on*, not as one more app. ## How this shapes the three arcs The arcs still compete; this lens sits over all of them: - [Capital efficiency](/arcs/capital-efficiency.md) → the *same rails* let one business unify margin and one consumer stretch collateral. One system, both. - [Risk relief](/arcs/risk-relief.md) → the risk engine is infrastructure a business runs its book on *and* a consumer relies on. Same guardian, both sides. - [Agentic credit](/arcs/agentic-credit.md) → "Morpho gives agents a market; Vanna gives them a balance sheet" is an *infrastructure* claim.

Vanna docs: Vanna includes borrowed funds already held or deployed in collateral where recognized.
Vanna docs: Vanna calculates displayed collateral headroom as max(0, collateral USD - 1.1 × debt USD).
Vanna docs: Vanna defines Net Available Collateral as nonnegative equity rather than immediately withdrawable funds.
Vanna docs: A priced account with debt becomes a liquidation candidate in Vanna when its Health Factor is at or below 1.1.
